q: The Newman projection shows butane viewed along the C2–C3 bond. Which conformation is drawn?
c: Eclipsed, with each CH<sub>3</sub> eclipsing an H
h: Find the front CH<sub>3</sub> and the back CH<sub>3</sub>, then estimate the dihedral angle between them. Are the back bonds lined up with the front bonds or in between them?
w: The back bonds sit between the front bonds, so the projection is staggered. The front CH3 points straight up and the back CH3 points straight down: a 180° dihedral angle. That is the anti conformation, the lowest-energy conformation of butane.
x: Gauche would put the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on neighboring positions, 60° apart; here they are on opposite sides of the circle.
In the totally eclipsed conformation the back CH<sub>3</sub> would sit directly behind the front CH<sub>3</sub>; the back bonds here are offset, so nothing is eclipsed.
An eclipsed conformation has every back bond hidden behind a front bond; this drawing is staggered.

q: Four conformations of butane about the C2–C3 bond are shown. Rank them from lowest to highest energy.
h: First sort staggered from eclipsed (eclipsing always costs torsional strain). Then, within each group, ask how close the two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are.
w: I is gauche (staggered, CH3/CH3 60°), II is totally eclipsed (CH3 behind CH3), III is anti (180°), IV is eclipsed with each CH3 behind an H. Staggered conformations are lower than eclipsed ones; anti beats gauche by about 3.8 kJ/mol of steric strain. Among the eclipsed forms, two CH3/H eclipsings (about 16 kJ/mol) cost less than a CH3/CH3 eclipsing plus two H/H (about 19 kJ/mol). Order: III < I < IV < II.
x: This places an eclipsed conformation (IV) below a staggered one (I); any eclipsed form carries torsional strain far larger than the 3.8 kJ/mol gauche penalty.
Gauche (I) is not lower than anti (III): bringing the CH<sub>3</sub> groups to 60° adds steric strain.
The totally eclipsed conformation (II), with CH<sub>3</sub> directly behind CH<sub>3</sub>, is the highest point on the butane energy curve, not IV.

q: The Newman projection shows 2-methylbutane viewed along the C2–C3 bond (C2 in front). Using the strain values in the table, what is the total strain energy of this conformation (relative to a hypothetical strain-free one)?
h: Pair each front bond with the back bond directly behind it. There are exactly three eclipsing pairs; add their costs.
w: Read the three eclipsed pairs: CH3 (top, front) with CH3 (top, back) = 11; CH3 (lower left, front) with H = 6.0; H (lower right, front) with H = 4.0. Total = 11 + 6.0 + 4.0 = 21 kJ/mol. The gauche value does not apply because nothing here is staggered.
x: 17 kJ/mol leaves out the H/H eclipsing; H/H eclipsing is still torsional strain and must be counted.
15 kJ/mol skips the CH<sub>3</sub>/H eclipsing between the lower-left front CH<sub>3</sub> and the H behind it.
26 kJ/mol treats the lower-left pair as a second CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> eclipsing, but the back carbon (C3) carries only one CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Three staggered conformations of 2-methylbutane about the C2–C3 bond are shown (C2 in front). A CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> gauche interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol. Which conformation is highest in energy, and by how much does it lie above the most stable one?
h: Find the single CH<sub>3</sub> on the back carbon in each drawing and count how many front CH<sub>3</sub> groups sit 60° from it.
w: The back carbon (C3) has one CH3. In I it lies between a front CH3 and the front H (one gauche); in II it lies between the front H and the other front CH3 (one gauche); in III it sits between both front CH3 groups (two gauche, anti to H). I and II are equal (3.8 kJ/mol); III has 7.6 kJ/mol. So III is highest, 3.8 kJ/mol above I (and II).
x: 7.6 kJ/mol is the total gauche strain in III, not the difference from I, which already has one gauche interaction (3.8 kJ/mol).
I has only one gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> interaction; III, with the back CH<sub>3</sub> between both front CH<sub>3</sub> groups, has two.
II and I each have one gauche interaction, so they have the same energy; II is not higher than I.

q: Which Newman projection represents 2-bromobutane viewed along the C2–C3 bond (C2 in front)?
h: Write out C2 and C3 of 2-bromobutane. List the three groups on C2 other than C3, and the three groups on C3 other than C2.
w: 2-Bromobutane is CH3–CHBr–CH2–CH3. C2 carries Br, CH3 (C1) and H; C3 carries CH3 (C4) and two H. Only I has a front carbon with Br, CH3, H and a back carbon with CH3, H, H.
x: II is BrCH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane: the bromine-bearing carbon has two H and the back carbon has two CH<sub>3</sub>.
III has two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on the back carbon, so it is 2-bromo-3-methylbutane (five carbons), not 2-bromobutane.
IV is BrCH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> viewed along C1–C2: 1-bromobutane, a constitutional isomer.

q: The Newman projection shows an alkane viewed along one C–C bond. What is the IUPAC name of the alkane?
h: Rebuild the condensed formula: front carbon with its three groups, bonded to back carbon with its three groups. Find the longest chain; number from the end nearer a branch.
w: Front carbon: CH bearing CH2CH3 and CH3. Back carbon: CH bearing two CH3. The molecule is (CH3)2CH–CH(CH3)–CH2CH3, C7H16. Longest chain = 5 carbons; numbering from the isopropyl end gives methyls at C2 and C3: 2,3-dimethylpentane.
x: A four-carbon parent misses the longest chain: the ethyl group extends the main chain to five carbons.
Numbering from the wrong end gives 3,4; the lowest locants are 2,3.
The molecule has seven carbons (front C, back C, ethyl, and three methyls); a hexane parent with two methyls would need eight.

q: Rotation about the C–C bond of ethane has a barrier of about 12 kJ/mol. This barrier is attributed mainly to
c: torsional strain in the eclipsed conformation
steric strain from H atoms pressed inside their van der Waals radii
angle strain from H–C–C angles bent away from 109.5°
partial breaking of the C–C σ bond during rotation
h: Ethane's hydrogens are small and far apart even when eclipsed. Which kind of strain comes from bonds being lined up, rather than atoms bumping?
w: In the eclipsed conformation each C–H bond is aligned with a C–H bond on the neighboring carbon; the electron pairs repel and the stabilizing σ(C–H)→σ*(C–H) overlap of the staggered form is lost. That energy cost is torsional strain, about 4.0 kJ/mol per H/H eclipsing (3 × 4.0 ≈ 12).
x: The eclipsed H atoms of ethane are about 2.3 Å apart, slightly outside the sum of their van der Waals radii, so steric strain is minor; that term matters for larger groups such as CH<sub>3</sub>.
Bond angles stay near tetrahedral during rotation about a single bond; angle strain arises in small rings, not in ethane.
The C–C σ bond is cylindrically symmetric, so rotation does not break or weaken it; the barrier comes from interactions among the C–H bonds.

q:
Which statements about the conformations of butane about the C2–C3 bond are correct?
I. The gauche conformation is staggered but has steric strain.
II. The anti conformation is lower in energy than gauche by about 3.8 kJ/mol.
III. At 25 °C, rotation is too slow for the anti and gauche conformers to interconvert.
IV. The two gauche conformations are mirror images and have the same energy.
h: Compare butane's largest rotational barrier (about 19 kJ/mol) with room-temperature thermal energy; conformers can be isolated only when the barrier is about 80 kJ/mol or more.
w: I is true: in gauche the CH3 groups are 60° apart and crowd each other, but no bonds are eclipsed. II is true: the gauche penalty is about 3.8 kJ/mol. III is false: barriers of about 15–19 kJ/mol are crossed billions of times per second at 25 °C. IV is true: the +60° and −60° gauche forms are nonsuperimposable mirror images of equal energy. Answer: I, II, and IV only.
x: Statement IV is also correct: the two gauche conformations (CH<sub>3</sub> groups at +60° and −60°) are mirror images, so they have identical energy.
Statement III is false; butane's rotational barriers are small, so conformers interconvert rapidly at room temperature and cannot be separated.
Statement II is also correct: anti is more stable than gauche by about 3.8 kJ/mol of steric strain.

q: Two staggered conformations of ethane-1,2-diol (HOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) are shown. In the gas phase, which conformation predominates, and why?
c: II, because an intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bond is possible only in the gauche form
I, because steric strain between the two OH groups is smallest when they are anti
I, because the two C–O bond dipoles cancel in the anti arrangement
II, because the gauche conformation has less torsional strain than the anti conformation
h: Butane prefers anti because its CH<sub>3</sub> groups only repel. What attractive interaction can two OH groups have when they are close together?
w: In the gauche form (II) the two OH groups are close enough for one O–H to hydrogen-bond to the other oxygen. That attraction outweighs the small steric cost, so II predominates, because of an intramolecular hydrogen bond. In the anti form the OH groups are too far apart to interact.
x: OH groups are small, so the gauche steric penalty is minor; it is outweighed by the intramolecular hydrogen bond available only in the gauche form.
Dipole cancellation does favor anti in the gas phase for 1,2-dihalides, but in the diol the hydrogen bond dominates, so the gauche form is preferred.
Both conformations are staggered, so neither has torsional strain; the preference must come from another interaction.

q: Heats of combustion per CH<sub>2</sub> group are given. An unstrained acyclic CH<sub>2</sub> releases 658.6 kJ/mol. What is the total ring strain of cyclobutane?
h: Find the extra heat released per CH<sub>2</sub>, then remember how many CH<sub>2</sub> groups the ring has.
w: Excess per CH2 = 686.2 − 658.6 = 27.6 kJ/mol. Cyclobutane has four CH2 groups: 4 × 27.6 = 110 kJ/mol of ring strain (angle strain from 90° angles plus torsional strain).
x: 27.6 kJ/mol is the strain per CH<sub>2</sub>; total ring strain multiplies by the four CH<sub>2</sub> groups in the ring.
88.8 kJ/mol uses cyclopentane (664.0) as the strain-free reference; the stem gives 658.6 kJ/mol as the unstrained value.
115 kJ/mol is the strain of cyclopropane: 3 × (697.1 − 658.6). Cyclobutane is the 686.2 row.

q: Cyclobutane is not planar; one carbon is folded about 25° out of the plane of the other three. What does this puckering accomplish?
c: It staggers neighboring C–H bonds to lower torsional strain, at the cost of slightly more angle strain
It lowers angle strain by opening the C–C–C angles from 90° toward the ideal 109.5°
It relieves steric strain between the 1,3-carbons, which move farther apart across the ring
It allows the ring carbons to rehybridize toward sp<sup>2</sup>, which shortens and strengthens the C–C bonds
h: In planar cyclobutane every C–H bond is eclipsed with its neighbor. What happens to the C–C–C angle when the ring folds?
w: Planar cyclobutane would have all eight C–H bonds eclipsed. Folding the ring partially staggers them, reducing torsional strain. The price is that the C–C–C angles shrink slightly below 90° (about 88°), so angle strain rises a little. The net effect is a lower-energy puckered ring.
x: Puckering makes the C–C–C angles slightly smaller (about 88°), not closer to 109.5°; angle strain increases a little.
The 1,3-carbons actually move closer together when the ring folds; the benefit comes from staggering the C–H bonds.
Ring carbons in cyclobutane remain sp<sup>3</sup>; puckering is a conformational change, not a change in hybridization.

q: Cyclopropane undergoes ring-opening reactions (for example, with H<sub>2</sub>/Ni) that do not occur with propane. The main reason is that cyclopropane
c: has bent, poorly overlapping C–C bonds and high ring strain
has sp<sup>2</sup>-hybridized carbons and a reactive C=C π bond, like propene
has staggered C–H bonds that weaken the ring C–C bonds
has axial hydrogens that crowd each other, as in a chair
h: Compare the 60° internuclear angle with the angle sp<sup>3</sup> orbitals prefer. How well can such orbitals overlap?
w: The C–C–C internuclear angle is 60°, far below 109.5°, so the sp3-like orbitals overlap off-axis in bent (banana) bonds. These bonds are weak, and the ring carries about 115 kJ/mol of angle and torsional strain that is released when the ring opens.
x: Cyclopropane has no π bond; its carbons are sp<sup>3</sup>-like with extra p character in the ring bonds, and it is a saturated C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.
All six C–H bonds in planar cyclopropane are eclipsed, not staggered; eclipsing adds torsional strain.
Axial and equatorial positions belong to chair cyclohexanes; cyclopropane is a flat ring.

q: Rank these C6H14 isomers from lowest to highest boiling point.
h: All three have the same molar mass. Which shape gives the largest contact area for London dispersion forces?
w: Isomeric alkanes differ only in shape. Branching makes a molecule more compact and spherical, reducing surface contact and London dispersion forces. Hexane (I, bp 69 °C) > 2-methylpentane (II, 60 °C) > 2,2-dimethylbutane (III, 50 °C). Order: III < II < I.
x: This is reversed: branching lowers, not raises, the boiling point of isomeric alkanes because it shrinks the surface area.
2,2-Dimethylbutane (III) is the most branched and most compact, so it boils lowest, below 2-methylpentane.
Unbranched hexane (I) has the largest surface area and the strongest dispersion forces, so it boils highest.

q: Which alkane defines a rating of 100 on the octane scale for gasoline?
h: The reference compound is highly branched and resists premature ignition (knocking). It is often called isooctane.
w: The octane scale is anchored by heptane (0) and 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (isooctane, 100). Highly branched alkanes burn smoothly under compression; straight-chain alkanes knock.
x: Octane is the straight-chain C<sub>8</sub> alkane; it knocks badly and has an octane number below zero, despite the name of the scale.
Heptane is the zero point of the octane scale, not the 100 point.
2-Methylheptane is only lightly branched and knocks readily; its octane number is far below 100.

q: In a petroleum refinery, catalytic cracking is used mainly to
c: break large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes for gasoline
separate crude oil into fractions by their boiling points
convert straight-chain alkanes into aromatic hydrocarbons for gasoline
remove sulfur compounds from crude oil fractions
h: Gasoline demand is higher than the amount of the C<sub>5</sub>–C<sub>10</sub> fraction found in crude oil. What process makes more of it from heavier fractions?
w: Catalytic cracking heats heavy fractions (such as gas oil) over zeolite catalysts, breaking C–C bonds to give smaller alkanes and alkenes in the gasoline range, plus small alkenes used as chemical feedstocks.
x: Separating crude oil by boiling point is fractional distillation, which does not break any bonds.
Converting alkanes into aromatics (and branched isomers) is catalytic reforming, a different refinery process.
Removing sulfur is hydrodesulfurization (hydrotreating), not cracking.

q: Which C8H18 isomer releases the least heat on complete combustion?
h: All isomers burn to the same products (8 CO<sub>2</sub> + 9 H<sub>2</sub>O). The isomer that starts lowest in energy releases the least heat. How does branching affect alkane stability?
w: Isomers that give the same combustion products differ in heat of combustion only by their own stability. Branched alkanes are more stable than unbranched isomers, so the most highly branched isomer, 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane, starts lowest in energy and releases the least heat.
x: Octane is the least branched isomer and the least stable, so it releases the most heat of these four.
2-Methylheptane has only one branch; it is less stable than the highly branched 2,2,3,3-tetramethylbutane and releases more heat.
3-Methylheptane has only one branch, so it releases more heat than the most branched isomer.

q: The rotational barrier about the C–C bond in propane is 14 kJ/mol. If each H/H eclipsing interaction costs 4.0 kJ/mol, what does one CH<sub>3</sub>/H eclipsing interaction cost?
h: In the eclipsed conformation of propane, list the three pairs of eclipsed bonds. How many are H/H, and how many involve the CH<sub>3</sub>?
w: Viewed along C1–C2, the front carbon (CH3) has three H; the back carbon (CH2) has CH3, H, H. Eclipsing gives one CH3/H pair and two H/H pairs: 14 = 2(4.0) + x, so x = 6.0 kJ/mol.
x: 4.7 kJ/mol divides the barrier evenly over three pairs, ignoring that the CH<sub>3</sub>/H pair costs more than an H/H pair.
10 kJ/mol subtracts only one H/H interaction; there are two H/H eclipsings in eclipsed propane.
2.0 kJ/mol would make a CH<sub>3</sub>/H eclipsing cheaper than H/H, which contradicts the larger size of CH<sub>3</sub>.

q: Two staggered conformations of 1,2-dichloroethane are shown. Which conformation has zero net dipole moment, and how does the fraction of the gauche form change on going from the gas phase to a polar solvent?
c: I; the gauche fraction increases in a polar solvent
I; the gauche fraction decreases in a polar solvent
II; the gauche fraction increases in a polar solvent
II; the gauche fraction decreases in a polar solvent
h: Add the two C–Cl bond dipoles as vectors in each conformation. Then ask which conformer a polar solvent stabilizes more.
w: In the anti form (I) the two C–Cl dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel, so I has μ = 0. In the gauche form (II) they partly add, so II is polar. A polar solvent stabilizes the polar conformer more through dipole–dipole solvation, so I is nonpolar, and the gauche fraction increases in a polar solvent.
x: A polar solvent preferentially stabilizes the polar gauche conformer, so its share goes up, not down.
The gauche conformer has the C–Cl dipoles at 60°, so they add to a net dipole; the dipoles cancel only in the anti form.
The gauche form is the polar one, not the nonpolar one, and polar solvents raise rather than lower its population.

q: Consider the staggered conformations of 2,3-dimethylbutane about the C2–C3 bond. A CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> gauche interaction costs 3.8 kJ/mol. How many gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> interactions does the most stable staggered conformation have, and how much more stable is it than the other staggered conformations?
h: C2 and C3 each carry two CH<sub>3</sub> and one H. Draw the Newman with the two H anti, then with H anti to CH<sub>3</sub>; count gauche CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> pairs.
w: With the two H atoms anti, each back CH3 sits between one front CH3 and the front H: 2 gauche interactions (7.6 kJ/mol). In either of the other two staggered conformations (H anti to CH3), one back CH3 sits between both front CH3 groups and the other is next to one: 3 gauche interactions (11.4 kJ/mol). The most stable has 2 gauche interactions and is 3.8 kJ/mol more stable.
x: With four CH<sub>3</sub> groups on two adjacent carbons, no staggered arrangement puts every CH<sub>3</sub> pair anti; at least two gauche interactions remain.
Placing the H atoms anti leaves two, not one, gauche interactions: each back CH<sub>3</sub> is gauche to one front CH<sub>3</sub>.
7.6 kJ/mol is the total gauche strain of the best conformer; the other staggered conformers have 11.4 kJ/mol, so the difference is 3.8 kJ/mol.

q: Which conformation of butane (about C2–C3) has steric strain but no torsional strain?
h: Torsional strain comes from eclipsed bonds. Which staggered conformation still brings the CH<sub>3</sub> groups close together?
w: Torsional strain requires eclipsing, so only staggered conformations are free of it. Of the staggered ones, gauche puts the CH3 groups 60° apart, close enough to cause steric strain (about 3.8 kJ/mol).
x: Anti has neither torsional strain (staggered) nor steric strain (CH<sub>3</sub> groups 180° apart).
The totally eclipsed conformation has both steric strain and large torsional strain.
Any eclipsed conformation has torsional strain from the lined-up bonds.
